title: the DSG mining tail

banner.title: The DSG MINING TAIL, R523: printed p. 53 (pdf 54) plus the claim continuation on printed p. 54 (pdf 55) - the placer value: only gold, silver or platinum can be placer-mined (copper, iron, mithril and gemstones impossible), the value following the normal page-51 quality determination then the 1d4-times-10 percentage of full value (10-40%); the smelting: one smelter-proficiency character runs the operation with unskilled workers under supervision, over a bellows-and-unmeltable-container setup with a coal (sometimes wood) fire, the smoke and smell making it almost impossible to conceal, and the underground rule that careless ventilation lets the fire consume all the oxygen; the finishing: gemstones rarely need smelting (occasional heat for crusted minerals), the gem cutter proficiency cutting and polishing at 2d20 stones per character per day (excavation usually greatly exceeding finishing), and the weekly 1d100 exceptional-stone check (a 00 unearths a stone worth 1d100 times the week's average value); the duration: the secret d100 man-weeks roll with the doubles ladder (doubles add a d100 of man-months, doubles again a d100 of man-years, repeating until a non-doubles roll; a month is four weeks, a year 48 weeks; 12 miners use 12 man-weeks per week) and the placer exception (doubles disregarded, always 1-100 man-weeks); the hazards: inherent, with success attracting problems almost automatically; and the claim: the right to remove mineral wealth, clear titles rare with rulers usually holding title, the mining charter (as little as 25 or 30%, more often 50%, a strong ruler always 50%) enforced by spies, surprise inspections, discreet observation or a ruler-employed smelter reporting the exact amounts, cheating punished usually by death (leniency never restoring the mine), and the wilderness continuation - the overnight land war among rulers with tribute and the winner-dependent claim recognition, the savage denizens raiding trespassers with cancellable charter-like monster agreements, no legal protection (the claim held by whoever can hold it), claim-jumpers in direct proportion to profitability, the rarely-working concealment (hiding the entrance with secret doors and brush, the tailings spread or dumped in water at the 25% mining rate, the chipping noise carrying to Underdark creatures, the bulette bust-in, the smelter smoke killing concealment), and the wealth-disposal risk of brazen moneychanger visits
banner.provenance: the DSG scan (archive.org item advanced-dungeons-dragons-1st-edition), pdf = printed + 1; the text read from the IA djvu OCR (djvu.txt lines ~6790-7060) with the pdf Acrobat-Capture layer as the second read (idx 125 = the printed pp. 52-53 window, idx 127 = the printed p. 54 window); the compiled-tables appendix has no reprint of this prose. A CLEAN-READ ROUND: both machine reads agree on every load-bearing number, and the only garbles are the standing OCR die-notation class (djvu "14100"/"4100" and Capture "ld4"/"dlOO"/"1-1 00" all reading as 1d100/1d4). The charter percentages multi-confirm: the djvu "5096" and the Capture "50%" both read as 50%, and both reads give the as-little-as 25-or-30% phrasing (pinned as 25 with the phrasing noted). The tailings 25% mining rate, the 2d20 finishing capacity, the 4-week month, the 48-week year, the 1-100 man-week placer cap and the exceptional-stone 1d100 weekly check with the 1d100-times-average value all appear identically in both reads. CATCH-UP: the exceptional-stone paragraph sits on printed p. 52 with no gap child of its own (it fell between the R521 products child and the R522 quality child) - it rides this round via the Finishing child flip, keeping the report lossless. The hireling loyalty section proper (child 133) starts the NEXT round at its printed p. 54 heading. The R519 placer/tunnel seam and the R521 Table 30 seam are noted; nothing auto-credits.
banner.sentinel: A prose round: no tables pin. The dice pin as consts per the R508 convention - the placer 1d4 x 10 percentage, the 2d20 finishing capacity, the secret d100 duration roll, and the weekly 1d100 exceptional-stone check with its 1d100-times-average value roll. The conveniences and thresholds pin as consts: the 4-week month, the 48-week year, the 1-100 man-week placer cap, the 25-or-30/50 charter shares, and the 25% tailings-scattering mining rate. The rest pins as prose bools: the placer metal restrictions, the one-smelter rule with its equipment and ventilation, the gem-cutter finishing, the doubles duration ladder with the placer exception and the man-week definition, the charter enforcement and cheating penalty, the wilderness war/denizen/no-legal-protection/claim-jumper hazards, the concealment problem set, and the wealth-disposal risk. The exceptional-stone catch-up is load-bearing: printed p. 52 prose with no child line, pinned under the Finishing child. The R519/R520/R521 seams are noted; nothing auto-credits.

prev_record: - R522 LANDED 2026-10-17: commit fbdd59f (census 445 -> 446,
pushed a8503d2..fbdd59f), THE DSG MINE PRODUCT QUALITY,
printed pp. 50-51 (pdf 51-52) - the metals rules: the ore
quality equals the coins producible from the metal mined
by a single miner in a week (the ore heavily mixed with
rock, the smelter proficiency processing it to pure
state, the rare pure-nugget vein), the Table 33 d10
quality grid for five metals (copper 100/200/250/300/
pure-vein rule (a 10 on the quality roll means roll again
- another 10 is a pure vein needing no smelting, 1-9
smelts normally), the unsmelted selling (no more than
25%, possibly 5%), and the iron equivalences (1000 coins
of iron = a full plate suit, 100 spear points, or 500
arrowheads); and the gemstones rules: the rough
unrecognized stones identified by miner or jeweler
proficiency after 1d6 turns of study, the Table 34
seventeen stone rows in stones-per-man-week and average
value (bloodstone 2d10 at 20 + 10d6 gp, amber 1d10 at
6d100 gp, onyx 3d10 at 10 + 10d6 gp, turquoise and agate
4d10 at 5d6 gp, aquamarine 1d10 at 10 x 5d6 gp, garnet
and alexandrite 1d10 at 100 x 1d4 gp, jade 2d10 at
10 x 5d6 gp, amethyst 1d10 at 100 x 1d6 gp, topaz 2d10 at
100 x 1d4 gp, jet 1d10 at 10 x 5d6 gp, opal 1d10/3 at
200 x 1d6 gp, ruby 1d10/3 at 200 x 1d8 gp, sapphire
1d10/4 at 200 x 1d8 gp, diamond 1d10/5 at 300 x 1d6 gp,
emerald 1d10/5 at 300 x 1d8 gp, the footnote rows rolling
1d10 divided by 3/4/5 and rounded up), the unfinished
selling (no greater than 25%, possibly 10%), and the
weekly value re-roll (the week's quality applying to all
miners that week, the miner count set before the rolls).
THE OCR-FAILURE LESSON: the garbles are text the OCR
layers simply failed - Table 33's copper and iron rows
were dropped by EVERY machine read (djvu, Capture, and
the appendix reprint alike), and Table 34's machine reads
lost the stone labels and shuffled the cells; both grids
were settled by Curtiss reading the physical pages via
screenshot (Android Power + Volume Down; scroll-capture
for tall grids), with the final contested cell - onyx
10 + 10d6 gp - settled by Curtiss's direct read after
vision passes wobbled the operator and die count. The
physical book outranks the scan (the R521 bloodstone
lesson, twice exercised). NOTE: amber appears in Table
34 but not in Table 32's gemstone list - pinned as
printed per the R517 never-repair lesson. Pinned as
rules/dsgmine4.h (prefix dnqt, verified free; 38 inlines

dice/sides/divisor and value add/mult/dice/sides).

consts.name: dnrvPlacerDice
consts.comment: the placer full-value roll is one die.

consts.name: dnrvPlacerSides
consts.comment: the placer full-value roll is 1d4, multiplied by 10 to give the percentage of full value.

consts.name: dnrvPlacerPctMult
consts.comment: the d4 result times 10 is the percentage of full value gained from a placer mine (10-40%).

consts.name: dnrvFinishDice
consts.comment: a character finishing stones rolls 2 dice of capacity per day.

consts.name: dnrvFinishSides
consts.comment: a given character can only finish 2d20 stones in a day.

consts.name: dnrvDurationDice
consts.comment: the duration roll is one die.

consts.name: dnrvDurationSides
consts.comment: the DM secretly rolls d100 at the start of the mining operation: the result is the man-weeks before depletion.

consts.name: dnrvMonthWeeks
consts.comment: each month is treated as four weeks when totalling a mine's longevity.

consts.name: dnrvYearWeeks
consts.comment: each year is treated as 48 weeks, or 12 months, when totalling a mine's longevity.

consts.name: dnrvCharterLowPct
consts.comment: a mining charter might claim as little as 25 or 30% of the mine's profit for the ruler (the low claim only from a weak-grasping ruler avoiding conflict).

consts.name: dnrvCharterCommonPct
consts.comment: a charter more often requires a 50% share, and a strong ruler always asks for 50% of the mine's products.

consts.name: dnrvTailingsMiningPct
consts.comment: if miners scatter the tailings to hide the mine, the rate of mining is no more than 25% of what it could be.

consts.name: dnrvPlacerMinWeeks
consts.comment: a placer mine is always depleted after 1 man-week of work at the minimum (doubles disregarded).

consts.name: dnrvPlacerMaxWeeks
consts.comment: a placer mine is always depleted after at most 100 man-weeks of work.

consts.name: dnrvExcepStoneDice
consts.comment: the exceptional-stone check is one die (the printed p. 52 catch-up).

consts.name: dnrvExcepStoneSides
consts.comment: roll 1d100 each week the mine is operating: a result of 00 means an exceptional stone is unearthed.

bools.name: dnrvPlacerGoldSilverPlatinumOnly
bools.comment: placer mining of copper, iron, mithril, or any kind of gemstone is impossible for these rules; only gold, silver, or platinum deposits can be worked with a placer mine.

bools.name: dnrvPlacerUsesQualityThenPercent
bools.comment: calculate the placer value by the normal quality determination (page 51), then apply the 1d4-times-10 percentage of full value.

bools.name: dnrvOneSmelterSuffices
bools.comment: as with mining, only one character with smelter proficiency is required to run a smelting operation; other, unskilled characters work under that character's supervision.

bools.name: dnrvSmelterNeedsHotFire
bools.comment: the smelting of ore requires a fairly extensive equipment collection: because a very hot fire is crucial, smelters must have a bellows system and several unmeltable containers to hold heated ore.

bools.name: dnrvMostMineralsNeedCoal
bools.comment: most minerals require a coal fire for smelting, but some can be smelted by wood fires.

bools.name: dnrvSmeltingImpossibleToConceal
bools.comment: a smelting operation produces much smoke and smell, so it is almost impossible to conceal.

bools.name: dnrvUndergroundSmeltingVentilation
bools.comment: if done underground, the ventilation of the smelting area must be carefully attended, or the smelting fire is likely to consume all the oxygen in the area.

bools.name: dnrvStonesRarelyNeedSmelting
bools.comment: gemstones rarely require the complicated procedures needed to smelt ore from rock, though occasionally heat removes excess minerals crusted around the gemstones.

bools.name: dnrvGemCutterFinishes
bools.comment: the usual finishing procedure requires a character with gem cutter proficiency to cut and polish the stones.

bools.name: dnrvExcavationExceedsFinishing
bools.comment: the rate at which stones can be excavated usually greatly exceeds the 2d20-per-day rate at which they can be finished.

bools.name: dnrvMineWealthFinite
bools.comment: a given mine always contains a finite amount of mineral wealth - occasionally a lifetime or more, much more frequently the mine plays out after a certain time.

bools.name: dnrvDoublesAddMonths
bools.comment: if the secret d100 duration roll yields doubles (e.g., 11, 22, 33), the mine has a much longer duration: roll d100 again and read the result as man-months, added to the weeks.

bools.name: dnrvDoublesAgainAddYears
bools.comment: if the second d100 roll also yields doubles, roll d100 a third time reading man-years; further doubles add more years until a roll comes up without doubles.

bools.name: dnrvManWeekPerMiner
bools.comment: a man-week is the amount of work one human miner performs in a week - 12 miners engaged on a mine use up 12 man-weeks of its lifetime every week.

bools.name: dnrvPlacerDisregardsDoubles
bools.comment: if the mine is a placer mine, disregard any doubles rolls for the duration of the find: always depleted after 1-100 man-weeks of work.

bools.name: dnrvHazardsInherent
bools.comment: any mining operation includes an inherent set of hazards, and a very successful operation attracts additional problems almost automatically - no free lunch for avaricious player characters.

bools.name: dnrvClaimIsRightToWealth
bools.comment: a claim is the miner's claimed right to remove mineral or gemstone wealth from the ground; with clear and undisputable legal title it is usually no problem initially.

bools.name: dnrvTitleUsuallyARuler
bools.comment: except in the most civilized and well-developed areas, a clear and undisputable title is uncommon; if anyone holds title to the land it is usually a king or other ruler with a selfish interest in its wealth.

bools.name: dnrvCharterPossible
bools.comment: a character might gain a mining charter from a ruler allowing mining of a given tract, with a hefty percentage of the mine's profit turned over to the ruler.

bools.name: dnrvRulerEnforcesShare
bools.comment: the ruler takes steps to insure the fair share: a spy among the miners, surprise inspections, discreet observation from a safe distance, or a smelter/finisher in the ruler's employ loyally reporting the exact amount processed.

bools.name: dnrvCheatingUsuallyDeath
bools.comment: a miner caught cheating his liege is usually punished by death; exceptional leniency might let the character live - perhaps retaining all body parts - but never to continue operating the mine.

bools.name: dnrvWildernessClaimFreeButHazardous
bools.comment: a claim on wilderness land is initially free of charter negotiation, but the land is wilderness because it is too savage for settlement or no useful purpose was discovered.

bools.name: dnrvLandWarOvernight
bools.comment: land thought worthless for centuries can become highly sought after when minerals are found: rulers war over it, and the winning ruler exacts tribute - PCs who aided the winner may continue operating with taxes; PCs who opposed the winner have little likelihood of recognized claims, at best fleeing with their lives and some small profit.

bools.name: dnrvSavageDenizensRaid
bools.comment: raiding monsters show no favor to PCs perceived as trespassing; intelligent monsters not inclined to take over operations may be negotiated with, charter-like, but chaotic monsters have little respect for agreements and might cancel one with no more notice than a battle-cry or surprise attack.

bools.name: dnrvNoLegalProtection
bools.comment: a wilderness claim has no legal protection: it is generally owned by whichever creature or party is most capable of holding it against interlopers.

bools.name: dnrvClaimJumpersProportional
bools.comment: the number of claim-jumpers climbs in direct proportion to the mine's profitability - considerable wealth attracts distant creatures or high-level characters whose only purpose is taking the mine by force.

bools.name: dnrvConcealmentRarelyWorks
bools.comment: attempting to conceal the mine is commonly attempted but rarely successful: it virtually never works in a settled area and has only a limited chance in the wilderness.

bools.name: dnrvConcealmentProblems
bools.comment: concealment requires hiding the entrance (secret doors, piles of brush and twigs), defeating the tailings giveaway (spreading them over a large area, or dumping into a river, lake, or deep pit - at the 25% mining rate), and the noise of chipping that carries clues especially to Underdark creatures.

bools.name: dnrvSmelterKillsConcealment
bools.comment: a mine located next to a smelter had better abandon all hope of concealment: the clouds of smoke and pervasive odor make it all but impossible except in the most remote and uninhabited areas.

bools.name: dnrvWealthDisposalRisky
bools.comment: even in complete secrecy, wealth disposal is a problem: brazenly converting 100 pounds of solid gold at the moneychanger raises eyebrows, and NPCs getting wind of a valuable claim may follow the characters back to their mine.

bools.name: dnrvExcepStoneWeeklyCheck
bools.comment: in addition to the week's base stone value, roll 1d100 each week the mine operates: a 00 means an exceptional stone is unearthed (the printed p. 52 catch-up, no gap child of its own).

bools.name: dnrvExcepStoneValueRoll
bools.comment: the exceptional stone's finder rolls 1d100 and multiplies the result by the average stone value for that week - e.g., a 20 gp turquoise average and a 68 yields a 1,360 gp stone.
